cia-0000119708:
A November 1953 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Brazil. Getulio Vargas was back in the presidency, and his populist program was running into economic headwinds. Less than a year later, his government would collapse around him.

The paper weighs Vargas's position and the forces gathering against him. Brazil, the giant of South America, mattered to Washington in every calculation about the hemisphere. Forecasts written this close to a leader's fall invite checking against the event. This one shows what the agency expected of Brazil's course while Vargas still held power and his dramatic end was still months away.
cia-0000124308: An April 1951 CIA document reports on American prisoners of war in Canton, the Chinese city now called Guangzhou. Captured men from the Korean fighting were moved through Chinese cities, and Canton was a major stop. The paper records what the agency knew of where those prisoners were. City sightings mattered because they confirmed that specific men were alive on specific dates, news that reached families through channels slower than the war itself.
cia-0000132208: Situation report 525, from January 1991, gives an oil update: the slick continues to move, the heading breaking off. Iraq's spill into the Gulf was becoming a weapon aimed at coasts and water supplies. The report tracks the slick's movement. The slick threatened desalination plants that supplied drinking water to Gulf cities, which turned an oil story into a water story within days of the spill.
cia-0000132308:
A rumor about Saddam Hussein seeking asylum abroad leads Situation Report 618 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. The report is dated February 5, 1991. The headline word is cut short in the record title, but its meaning is plain.

Talk of the Iraqi leader fleeing circulated as the ground war drew close. Diplomats and reporters traded versions of the story across several capitals. In the event, Saddam stayed in Baghdad and held power after the war ended. The report preserves the rumor as analysts heard it at the time. That makes it a useful record of the uncertainty surrounding his intentions that winter.
cia-0000132608: Colombia's position on the Cuban issue fills item 2 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 4, 1960. Bogota was charting a careful middle course between Washington and Havana at that point. Within about a year Colombia would break with Cuba outright. The short item reports the position as it stood that summer.
cia-0000135908: Dated 2 May 1954, a declassified CIA document deals with the present status and likely future course of PBSUCCESS, weighed weeks before D-day. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136208: Dated 1 May 1954 and now declassified, a CIA cable records refugees leaving WSBURNT, people already moving before the invasion had even begun. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136308: Guidance on two fallback schemes fills this 25 June 1954 LINCOLN cable for CADICK. Plan Alpha turns on a strike at Matamoros, whose result should show whether that plan goes ahead and how. Plan Beta applies if Alpha's answer is negative and the current combat engagement stalls; then Beta must be implemented. Written late in the PBSUCCESS fighting, the short cable lays out headquarters' branching logic for the operation's next move.
cia-0000136908: A weakened dock is the best sabotage target, this April 1954 cable argues. If many arms now sit on it, the dock is both valuable and exposed. It holds cargo for loading and onward movement. Attacking the ship makes no point if most cargo is gone. Strong efforts run on another track too. The Swedish government is being pressed. So is the British chartering company. Both are asked to recall the ship before unloading ends.
un-sc-res-108:
Talks meant to calm the Egypt-Israel armistice line broke down in 1955, and fighting flared up along the line drawn on 24 February 1949. Resolution 108, adopted without dissent on 8 September 1955, responds to a report from the Chief of Staff of the UN Truce Supervision Organization in Palestine.

The Council notes with approval that both sides accepted the Chief of Staff's call for a cease-fire with no conditions. It tells both sides to restore order, keep the cease-fire in full force, and pull their forces clearly apart, as he proposed. UN observers must be free to move in the area, and each side must name people to work with him.
un-sc-res-1808: From 2008 comes Resolution 1808, a Security Council decision kept in official-record form in this collection. The text's authority flows from its adoption by fifteen members under the Charter. Its form is the familiar one, preamble then operative paragraphs, and the entry preserves both in full through the Wikisource transcription of the record.
un-sc-res-2008: Security Council Resolution 2008 is held in this collection as a transcription of the official record from English Wikisource. The members who adopted it acted within the Council's standing charge over peace and security. Their complete text is the entry: the shared account of the matter first, then the shared decision that followed from it.
cia-0000132508: One of several CIA briefings on Cuba dated February 4, 1961, this paper adds another entry to the pre-invasion reporting flow. Multiple Cuba papers were produced that same week, as the agency fed a new president weighing the exile landing plan. Declassified years later, the document survives through the CIA Reading Room mirror held by the Internet Archive, where its place in the February rush is part of its meaning.
cia-0000135608: Dated 4 January 1961, this document in Spanish comes from the declassified files of Brigade 2506, the CIA-trained Cuban exile force. By January the brigade was deep in training for the landing that came three months later at the Bay of Pigs. The catalog names no topic for this item. It is kept in its original Spanish, as released through the CIA Reading Room: a single dated piece of exile paperwork whose substance has to be read in the text itself.
cia-0000135708: Dated 6 January 1961, a Spanish paper from the declassified files of Brigade 2506. The exile brigade was in training for the April landing in Cuba, an operation run by the CIA and hidden from the public. The record states no subject for this document. It is held in its original Spanish, one of many similar items the brigade produced that winter, and it is described here by date and provenance alone.
plos-pone-0000008:
Maxim Kapralov and Dmitry Filatov studied evolution in one of its classic island settings for a 2006 PLOS ONE paper. Schiedea is a plant genus found only in Hawaii, where one ancestor split into many species suited to different niches. That rapid split is called adaptive radiation.

The authors read the plants' DNA for signs of molecular adaptation, changes in genes driven by natural selection during the radiation. Finding which genes changed, and how fast, shows adaptation at work at the level of molecules, not just shapes and habits. Island groups like Schiedea are natural experiments, and this study checks the experiment's results gene by gene.
cia-0000137108: The 2506 Brigade's Spanish papers include this text, dated only to 1960 in the catalog. The brigade was the CIA-trained exile force that would land at the Bay of Pigs the following spring. The record gives no month or subject for the item. It is preserved in the original Spanish in the declassified release, one of the brigade's first-year documents, held for readers to examine in full.
cia-0000137308: NSC Briefing — Cuba, dated 1960, is a declassified CIA paper for the National Security Council, the president's top security advisory body. Its title names the whole of its known subject: Cuba, in the year the new revolutionary government and the United States moved from friction to open hostility. Other briefings with the same title survive from both 1960 and 1961, and the catalog does not distinguish this one's contents. It is preserved as released through the CIA Reading Room, a single dated briefing in a much larger Cuba file.
alexander-locke-1908:
Samuel Alexander wrote this short study of John Locke for the Philosophical Classics series, and it appeared in 1908. Alexander taught at Manchester and later won fame as a thinker in his own right. His subject was the English thinker whose work shaped modern ideas about knowledge, government, and faith.

Readers get Locke's life in brief, then a clear tour of his main claims. Minds start blank, Alexander explains, and all knowledge grows from sense and reflection. In politics, Locke held that rule rests on consent and that people keep rights no ruler may take. The book stays a neat first map of a thinker who helped found liberal thought.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d108: Charles Bohlen, First Secretary at the Moscow embassy, wrote a memorandum dated November 9, 1943, preserved as Document 108 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Bohlen, a Russian speaker, was becoming the American government's sharpest interpreter of Soviet affairs, and his memoranda fed the Tehran briefings. The record gives the author and the date only. The paper is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d208:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson wrote a personal, confidential letter to Harry Hopkins, the President's special assistant, on 10 November 1943. Stimson says he has reflected on their talk of the day before and wants his views on paper, in case they help Hopkins or Roosevelt at the coming conferences.

His first point is Overlord, the planned invasion of France: preparations are on schedule, and any slip to midsummer would cost many thousands of lives, so Roosevelt must hold firm against diversions. Second, General Marshall must command Overlord himself, and soon. Third, no new chief of staff should be named yet; an acting chief can hold the post while Marshall is in London.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d308:
A revised American draft of the Cairo communiqué, dated 25 November 1943, was dictated by Harry Hopkins to Warrant Officer Cornelius that morning. It folds Roosevelt's handwritten changes into the draft of the day before, and it names the conference's members from all three delegations.

In joint-statement form, the text says the leaders have agreed on future military operations against Japan from China and Southeast Asia, promising continuous and ever stronger offensives. Pacific islands seized by Japan will be taken from her forever. Territory stolen from China, such as Manchuria and Formosa, will return to the Republic of China. All lands taken by violence and greed will be freed. Korea, in due time after Japan's fall, will become free and independent.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d408:
A first draft of the Tehran communiqué, undated and apparently an American paper, is printed here with its handwritten changes shown. An editorial headnote states that no evidence has been found of the draft being considered outside the American delegation. The sense of its third paragraph was, though, discussed at the plenary meeting of 30 November.

The draft has the three leaders declare their determination. Their nations are to work together in war and in the peace that follows. Complete agreement is claimed on the scope and timing of operations from east, west, and south. A direct address to the German people follows: We do not seek to enslave you, it says. But we mean to destroy your armies, your submarines, and your war plants from the air, relentlessly. Roosevelt's own hand supplied several of the strongest word changes, and Hopkins added the leaders' names at the end.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d508:
The Combined Administrative Committee reported to the Combined Chiefs of Staff in this paper dated December 15, 1943, a little over a week after the Second Cairo Conference. Administrative officers handled the supply, transport, and services side of the joint war effort. The State Department printed the report in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Grand strategy fails without administration: divisions need ports, fuel, food, and shipping space before they can fight. A committee report of this kind shows the logistical reckoning that followed Cairo's decisions. For readers, it offers the working underside of the summit, where the fine phrases of communiqués were tested against tonnage tables and supply lines.
frus-1944-quebec-d108:
Harry Hopkins, President Roosevelt's special assistant, sent this top-secret memorandum to Admiral William Leahy, the president's chief of staff, on September 7, 1944. It weighs in on a Joint Chiefs of Staff paper about what should happen to lend-lease material once Germany was beaten. Hopkins wrote days before Roosevelt and Churchill met at Quebec.

Hopkins argued the paper should not be approved. He pointed to the lend-lease agreements, which promised return of goods only at the end of the whole emergency, not after Germany alone fell. He also cited the shared munitions pool agreed with Britain. Acting alone, he warned, would stir needless friction with allies while Japan still had to be fought.
frus-1944-quebec-d208:
The Combined Chiefs took up the zones paper, C.C.S. 320/26, on September 16, 1944, and approved it with minor amendments as C.C.S. 320/27. Cunningham secured agreement that naval disarmament in American-controlled ports would sit with the American naval member of the Control Commission. He also suggested the American area include Bremerhaven, downriver from Bremen, where large ships berth.

Somervell noted American troops might also be supplied through Antwerp and Rotterdam, and raised an Inter-Allied commission for the Rhine. Logistics went to the Combined Administrative Committee. The meeting also approved Mediterranean "Rankin" planning and release of amphibious craft from Overlord. Marshall then reported Stilwell's news: Japanese advancing on Kweilin, and Chiang still refusing Stilwell command of all Chinese forces.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d108:
Three zones and one shared capital: that is the map this protocol draws for beaten Germany. Signed by the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union on 12 September 1944, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It carries out the surrender instrument's article on occupation.

Germany, inside her frontiers of 31 December 1937, is split for occupation into three zones, one for each power. Berlin forms a special area held jointly by all three. The protocol then spells out each boundary in surveyor's detail.
