frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1308:
Stimson answered Harrison on 21 July 1945, writing from the summit to the acting chairman of the Interim Committee. The reply direction shows the channel working both ways. The war secretary directed the atomic file from Potsdam while the committee's work went on in Washington.

A secretary's note to his acting chairman could carry rulings, questions, or word of the talks that bore on the bomb. Stimson held the whole thread in his own hands that week. This message is his end of it. It shows the atomic policy being run by letter between two men who shared its full secret.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1408:
Caffery's run of cables to Secretary Byrnes continues with a third dated 6 August 1945. Paris was then pressing Washington on France's role in the German settlement. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Three cables to the secretary in a single day is the mark of a post that believes its hour has come. The Potsdam powers had drawn Germany's zones without France; Paris wanted in, and Caffery carried that want to Washington. His cluster of cables lets readers feel the weight of paper a determined embassy could pile on a secretary's desk. The volume's French section turns on days like this one.
frus-1945-50-intel-d108:
Director of Central Intelligence Souers wrote to Quinn of the SSU on 4 April 1946, the day after the War Department's letter to Quinn. The new chief and the old unit were now in direct dealing. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Letters between the rising body and the remnant it would absorb have a special tone: courteous, exact, and final. Souers needed the SSU's stations and officers; Quinn needed terms for his people. Readers can watch the transfer being negotiated chief to chief. Within months the SSU's secret work passed to the CIG, giving the group the operational arm its charter had lacked. This letter is an early instrument of that passing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d208:
A memorandum dated 5 March 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Chief of the Legislative Liaison Division, Central Intelligence Group (Pforzheimer). The reader was the Deputy Director of Central Intelligence (Wright). The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 208 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d308:
A memorandum dated 6 January 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Director of the Policy Planning Staff, Department of State (Kennan). The reader was the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, Central Intelligence Agency (Wisner). It stands as document 308 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. It was a season of stock-taking: the CIA was a year old, and its friends and critics were both writing things down.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. The points are stated once and left to stand; the file around it holds the answer they drew. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d408:
Brigadier General John Magruder wrote to Secretary of Defense Louis Johnson on 22 December 1949. His memo is document 408 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Magruder had led the wartime Strategic Services Unit, a bridge between the old OSS and the new CIA. He knew secret work from the inside and spoke with rare weight on it. A memo from him to the Secretary of Defense brings a soldier's view into the debate over the young agency. Magruder's voice carried the memory of wartime secret work into a peacetime fight over its future.
frus-1861-d108:
On 19 October 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The letter is document 108 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote to Welles and to Lyons on the same day, a neat picture of his craft. The home note aligned the Navy, the foreign note faced the British envoy. Both letters serve one aim: a blockade that held in law as well as at sea. One aim, two letters: the pairing shows Seward's craft at its most neat. Craft of that neat kind is easy to miss and hard to praise too much.
frus-1861-d208:
Mr. Wood reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 19 July 1861. The printed record keeps it as Document 208 in the President's message volume for 1861. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d308:
Mr. Bigler reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 2 September 1861. The printed record keeps it as Document 308 in the President's message volume for 1861. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d108:
Writing from Washington on 24 July 1862, William H. Seward addressed Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 108 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d208:
Dated 13 February 1862, Document 208 is a note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. It is preserved in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume, the printed record of the year in American diplomacy.

That week Union forces were taking Fort Donelson, a victory that opened the Tennessee River. Victories abroad-minded men in London and Paris read such news closely, since a short war meant less pressure to step in. Seward's steady stream of notes to Lyons kept the Union's reading of events in front of the British legation in this season. Britain's first concern in Washington was the blockade and what it cost British trade.
frus-1862-d308:
On 25 August 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote once more to William L. Dayton in Paris, in a dispatch printed as Document 308 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Seward wrote four days before the second battle of Bull Run opened, in a capital tense with rumors of Lee's movements. His letter to Paris closed the pre-battle mail. Within weeks, the defeat's echo in Europe would make letters like this one. With their calm statement of Union purpose, the baseline from which Washington argued its case. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d408:
On 18 August 1862, soon after Gustav Koerner took up the post of American minister to Spain, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to him. It is Document 408 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Koerner, a German-born Illinois lawyer and friend of Lincoln, replaced Carl Schurz at Madrid in the middle of the war. His brief was delicate: keep Spain neutral, guard Union interests in Cuba, and watch French designs on Mexico. An early instruction from Seward set out the line the new minister was to hold. It marks the handover of the Madrid mission at a tense point in the war.
frus-1862-d508:
On 9 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. It is Document 508 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Seward wrote just after McClellan's retreat from Richmond, when the Union's case in Europe needed repair. His July orders to the posts abroad supplied the government's account of the campaign and its unaltered resolve. At The Hague, Pike had to turn that account into answers for Dutch officials and editors. The instruction is part of the damage-control file of midsummer 1862. In that file Seward refused to let a lost campaign become a lost argument in Europe.
frus-1862-d608:
On 15 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Thomas Corwin in Mexico. It is Document 608 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Seward wrote two days before Antietam, in the round of orders that went to posts across the world that week. For Mexico the line was unchanged but not empty. The United States still recognized only the Juárez government. It still rejected the European design on its neighbor. Corwin had to make that position felt in a capital where French bayonets were the daily argument against it. The letter shows the Union's Mexican policy holding its shape under maximum strain.
frus-1862-d708:
On 18 September 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to James R. Partridge, an American envoy in Central America. The letter is document 708 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. It answers Partridge's dispatch of late August.

Answers from Washington told an envoy how his reports had landed and what to do next. Seward's letter to Partridge kept a small post in step with the government's aims for the isthmus and its routes. Kept in the printed volume, it shows that no post was too small for the secretary's eye. That held in the fall of 1862, even with the war at its height.
frus-1863p1-d108:
William H. Seward closed his great batch with this twelfth letter to Charles Francis Adams dated 2 March 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 108 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Twelve letters in a day capped the winter's work on the London file. Seward sent Adams into the spring with each head of the brief fresh on its own sheet. This letter is the last of the dozen, the tail of the most packed day in the printed exchange. It rounds off a set that still shows how a war was run, in part, from one man's desk.
frus-1863p1-d208:
The Secretary of State, William H. Seward, wrote to his minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 24 May 1863. The letter is document 208 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d308: A letter from a Mr. Wise to a Mr. Stuart, dated 18 October 1862, appears as document 308 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart served at the British legation in Washington, and the paper belongs to the volume's Anglo-American correspondence from the Civil War. The record supplies no first names, so the two surnames and the date are the firm facts.
frus-1863p1-d408:
On 3 March 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 408 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Cases in these notes can look small, one ship or one arrested man, yet each tested the rules of neutrality. Both governments treated the precedents as serious business. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d508:
Writing on 12 May 1863, William H. Seward, Secretary of State addressed Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington in an official letter. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d608:
A dispatch dated 12 August 1863 went from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
plos-pbio-0020008:
Elena Rebollo, Salud Llamazares, José Reina, and their team studied cell division in the fruit fly for PLOS Biology in 2004. When a cell divides, a spindle of tiny tubes pulls the chromosomes apart. In fly sperm-forming cells, some of those tubes grow without the usual organizing centers, called centrosomes.

The question was whether those extra tubes truly help build the spindle or are just bystanders. The study shows they do real work in getting the spindle into shape. That widens the standard picture of division, which gives centrosomes the lead role. Knowing all the ways a spindle can form helps explain why division is so robust, and why it fails in some diseases.
plos-pbio-0020108:
Eric Bair and Robert Tibshirani presented a statistics method in PLOS Biology in 2004. Doctors want to predict how long cancer patients will live using gene activity data. The catch is that such data sets hold thousands of genes but few patients, so plain methods often fail.

Their semi-supervised approach first finds gene patterns tied to outcome without using survival times, then links those patterns to survival. Splitting the task this way cuts the noise that swamps direct methods. Better survival forecasts help doctors sort patients by risk and choose how hard to treat. The paper is a good example of math built for the exact shape of a real data problem.
plos-pbio-0020408:
Linus T.-Y. Tsai, Roland J. Bainton, Justin Blau, and their team linked clock neurons to drug response in flies in PLOS Biology in 2004. Fruit flies with faults in a gene called Lmo behave oddly after cocaine exposure. The authors traced part of that effect to the pacemaker neurons that run the fly's daily clock.

Clock neurons were thought to keep time and little else. Here they also shape how strongly a fly responds to a drug. That overlap hints that time-of-day systems and addiction pathways share parts. It may help explain why drug sensitivity varies across the day. The fly gives a simple system for testing such links gene by gene.
plos-pone-0000108:
Nikos Oikonomou, Vaggelis Harokopos, Jonathan Zalevsky, and their team traced a lung disease step in PLOS ONE in 2006. Lung inflammation can heal cleanly or turn into fibrosis, stiff scar tissue that blocks breathing. The signal TNF is a known driver of inflammation, and it comes in a free-floating, soluble form.

The team shows the soluble form is the one that pushes inflamed lung tissue over into fibrosis. That split matters for therapy, since anti-TNF drugs exist but carry risks. Aiming only at the soluble form might keep the benefit and drop some harm. The finding gives lung fibrosis, a disease with few good treatments, a precise target to test.
plos-pone-0000208:
Gidske L. Andersen and Knut Krzywinski published this desert ecology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tracks desert trees in a hyper-arid environment, among the driest places on Earth. The authors measure mortality, recruitment of young trees, and overall population change.

In a hyper-arid desert, a tree population can hang on rare rains or quietly die out. Long-term counts of deaths and new recruits show which way the balance tips. The work matters for predicting how extreme drylands and their sparse tree cover will respond as climates shift. Long-term records like this are rare in deserts this dry.
plos-pone-0000308:
Heather A. Piwowar, Roger S. Day, and Douglas B. Fridsma published this research policy paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It asks whether sharing detailed research data pays off for the sharer. The authors report, as the title says, that sharing is associated with an increased citation rate for the papers whose data are shared.

Citations are the currency of academic reward, so a citation boost is a real incentive. The study measured that association across a set of shared datasets. It became a frequently cited piece of evidence in the open science movement's case for mandatory data sharing.
plos-pone-0000408:
Mitsumasa Yoda, Kohei Eguchi, and Tomoki P. Terada dissected the protein clock that ticks inside cyanobacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2007. These bacteria keep a daily rhythm using just three proteins, with KaiC at the center, cycling through chemical states over about 24 hours. The team studied how KaiC units shuffle and switch shape.

They describe monomer-shuffling, where KaiC subunits swap between complexes, and an allosteric transition, a shape change that alters the protein's activity. Together these motions may keep the clock's period steady. A clock built from so few parts is a gift for physics-minded biology: every moving piece can, in principle, be accounted for.
plos-pone-0000508:
W. John Kress and David L. Erickson proposed a standard DNA barcode for identifying land plants, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. A barcode is a short DNA stretch that differs between species, letting a sample be named from a leaf fragment or seed. Their two-locus barcode pairs the coding gene rbcL with the non-coding spacer region trnH-psbA.

One locus alone mislabels too many plant species; the pair complements each other, one steady and one variable. A working plant barcode serves ecology, customs checks on traded timber and herbs, and the cataloging of unknown floras. The paper helped settle a practical standard that later global efforts built on.
plos-pone-0000608:
Olivier Delelis and colleagues studied how HIV's copying enzyme cuts DNA at a specific pattern, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. HIV-1 integrase inserts the virus's DNA into the host genome, a step drugs can block. The team showed efficient and specific internal cleavage of a retroviral palindromic DNA sequence by tetrameric HIV-1 integrase, the four-part form of the enzyme.

A palindrome reads the same both ways, and the viral DNA ends carry such patterns. Showing the four-part enzyme cuts there specifically clarifies the exact reaction integrase inhibitors must stop. Mechanistic detail of this kind underlies the design of a major class of HIV drugs.
plos-pone-0000708:
Yoshihito Niimura and Masatoshi Nei tallied the gains and losses of smell genes across mammal evolution, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Smell in mammals runs on a large family of olfactory receptor genes. Their number varies extensively among species. Most species also carry many pseudogenes, broken copies that no longer work.

The title reports extensive gains and losses in this family over evolutionary time. Lineages that live by smell keep or expand their receptor sets, while others let them decay. Comparing counts and pseudogenes across species turns the family into a record of how each mammal makes its living. It also sharpens questions about why humans kept the sense they did.
plos-pone-0000808:
Sébastien Gingras, Stéphane Pelletier, Kelli Boyd and colleagues characterized a new family of nuclear proteins first spotted in activated T cells. Gene array analysis had been widely used to find genes switched on during T cell activation. Their studies identified an immediate early gene strongly induced by IL-2 in mouse T cells, which they named CSRNP-1, for cysteine-serine-rich nuclear protein-1. A human counterpart followed.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE paper characterizes the whole CSRNP family. Proteins rich in cysteine and serine, sitting in the nucleus, and switched on within hours of activation look like regulators of the response program. Naming and mapping a family is the first step toward learning what it controls.
plos-pone-0000908:
Luciana Girao, Ariadna Lopes, Marcelo Tabarelli and colleagues studied how breaking up Atlantic Forest changes tree reproduction, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A forest's mix of working traits helps keep the whole system running. How human disturbance scrambles that mix was poorly known.

The team tested whether fragmentation shifts which reproductive traits dominate among trees. Fragmented edges favor some pollination and seed styles over others, thinning the range of strategies. A narrower range can leave a forest less able to recover from drought or disease. The study gives conservationists a trait based way to judge forest damage, beyond counting species alone.
plos-pone-0001008:
Luis Santamaria, Javier Rodriguez-Perez, Asier Larrinaga and colleagues predicted where new plants arise from how animals move, in PLOS ONE in 2007. For plants spread by fruit eating animals, recruitment patterns start with where parent plants stand. They are then reshaped by how the animal digests seeds, where it travels and how the land is laid out.

The team use animal displacement kernels, math descriptions of how far seeds are carried, to predict spatial patterns of new plants. Such predictions help judge whether a plant population can track a shifting climate. They also show how losing a seed carrier can quietly rewrite a forest map.
plos-pone-0001108:
Chiara Begliomini, Andrea Caria, Wolfgang Grodd and colleagues compared grasping in natural and constrained movements, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In monkeys, grasping relies on a circuit between a parietal area called AIP and premotor area F5. Single cell recordings there show how the brain turns sight of an object into a shaped hand.

Human studies often force unnatural, constrained grasps for the scanner. The team compare those with natural movements to find what changes. If the circuit behaves differently under constraint, scanner results need care when read as daily grasping. The paper is a methods check with direct bearing on brain imaging of hand control.
plos-pone-0001208:
Invasive species usually get blamed on trade and travel, which carry organisms around the world. Wen Lin and colleagues added a less obvious driver in a 2007 PLOS ONE article: fast economic development within a country. They tested the idea using China as their case.

Using principal factor analysis, the authors explored how development intensity relates to the pace of biological invasions. Indirect factors that raise invasion pressure had rarely been quantified. Their finding suggests that as economies grow and build, they open more doors to foreign species, a cost of development that planning rarely counts.
plos-pone-0001308:
Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 is a probiotic strain used for gut disorders. Sya Ukena and colleagues studied how it affects a leaky gut, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The intestinal barrier is formed by gut lining cells and the junctions between them, and it keeps contents where they belong. Disruption raises permeability. It is also a key mechanism in gut infections.

The authors report that the probiotic inhibits leaky gut by enhancing mucosal integrity. Probiotics are proposed to positively modulate this barrier, and their study tests one strain's mechanism directly. The result supports a specific claim for a widely sold probiotic.
plos-pone-0001408:
Jörn Scharlemann and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a new way to clean satellite data for ecology. Satellites track land cover, heat, and plant growth over time. Such series help model where plants and animals live, most of all those of farm or wild life value. Raw series are noisy, so they must be smoothed with care.

The authors present a fresh method based on wave like fits over time. It aims to keep true seasonal shifts while cutting noise. Clean data matter, since maps built from them guide land and health choices. Their method gives field teams a sharper tool for work that spans years and wide areas.
plos-pone-0001508:
Paolo Monaci and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on picking useful antibodies fast. Labs build vast antibody sets and must find ones that bind targets with a set pattern. The usual search needs facts that may not exist. The team built a tag based array method to screen the sets by gene chip.

Short DNA tags mark each antibody clone in the set. Chips then read which clones bind which targets in one pass. That speed lets teams mine huge sets without slow one by one tests. The method could cut the cost of finding antibodies for research and care.
plos-pone-0001608:
Rita Neres and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on malaria in pregnancy in mice. Malaria in pregnancy brings grave harm: sicker mothers, poor fetal growth, low birth weight, and infant deaths. Its course in women is hard to study in depth. The team infected pregnant mice with a rodent malaria strain.

The mouse course closely copied the harm seen in pregnant women, down to womb tissue changes. A close copy gives labs an ethical way to test drugs and shots for this group. Pregnant women are oft left out of trials, so a sound model holds extra value. It may speed guards for a group at sharp risk.
plos-pone-0001708:
Zoe Waibler, Linda Y. Sender, Camilla Merten, and their co-authors profiled powerful immune-activating antibodies in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Superagonistic CD28 antibodies switch T cells on without the usual co-signal from the T-cell receptor complex. In rodents they expand regulatory T cells and can treat autoimmune disease. In a human trial, though, such an antibody caused severe harm, making its signals a safety question.

The team mapped the signaling signatures and functional properties of anti-human CD28 superagonists. The full text gives the cell tests and which pathways fired. Knowing exactly what these antibodies do in human cells is a precondition for any safe return of the class. It is also a case study in how animal results can mislead.
plos-pone-0001808:
Michael B. Gill, Rachel Edgar, Janet S. May, and their co-authors studied how a herpesvirus spreads between cells in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Viruses cannot propel themselves. To move within multi-cellular hosts they must manipulate infected cells. Herpesviruses are a model for such manipulation, but most movement knowledge covered alpha-herpesviruses, leaving the gamma group understudied.

The team reports that a gamma-herpesvirus glycoprotein complex manipulates actin, the cell's internal scaffolding, to promote viral spread. The full text gives the cell imaging and the spread assays. A virus that remodels the cell's skeleton to travel is harder to stop with antibodies alone, which aim at free virus particles.
plos-pone-0001908:
Kelly Salter and co-authors built a way to pick breast cancer drugs per patient, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. A core problem in cancer care is choosing the drug most likely to work for one person. A drug that fails still costs time, health, and quality of life, so a test that sorts patients first has real value.

The team joined several kinds of patient data into one approach to forecast how a tumor would respond to chemotherapy. A sound forecast lets doctors skip drugs bound to fail and start with the best bet. The study is a step toward cancer care matched to each tumor, rather than one plan for all.
plos-pone-0002008:
Jorge Zavala and co-authors studied how a caterpillar's gut copes with a plant's chemical defense, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The plant, a wild tobacco, makes trypsin proteinase inhibitors, proteins that block the gut enzymes of insects that eat it. Past work had shown these blockers defend the plant, by changing their levels in the plant and watching the caterpillar suffer.

The team now looked inside the caterpillar, the hornworm Manduca sexta, at its midgut proteinases, the enzymes that digest food. If the worm answers blockers by changing its enzymes, the plant defense is a moving duel. The study maps both sides of that duel.
plos-pone-0002108:
Chit-Ming Wong and co-authors asked whether exercise guards against death in flu seasons, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Little was known about the effect of physical exercise on influenza-associated mortality, the extra deaths that come with flu waves. The team collected data on exercise habits, other lifestyle traits, and social and economic status.

Their data cover the underlying cause of death of twenty-four thousand six hundred fifty-six adults, most aged sixty-five or older. A link, if real, would add flu survival to the long list of exercise gains. The study gives a careful test in a very large group.
plos-pone-0002208:
Daniel Ramot, Brandon Johnson, Tommie Berry, and co-authors built a machine to watch worms move, described in PLOS ONE in 2008. The tiny worm Caenorhabditis elegans is a workhorse for studying behavior, nerve signaling, and muscle. Most studies of its crawling relied on a human observer's judgment, which is slow and hard to repeat.

The Parallel Worm Tracker films many worms at once and measures their speed automatically. It can also score drug-induced paralysis, a standard test in worm labs. Automating the watching turns a chore into clean data, letting genetics and drug studies run at a much larger scale.
plos-pone-0002308:
Andrew Pask, Kerry McInnes, David Webb, and co-authors tested a topical estrogen treatment on human foreskin tissue, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. With HIV still spreading, simple and cheap new prevention methods are badly needed. Male circumcision cuts a man's risk of infection by about 60 percent, probably because it removes tissue rich in Langerhans cells. This HIV uses to enter the body.

The team asked whether estrogen cream could keratinise the foreskin, thickening its surface layer, instead of surgery. A tougher surface may block the virus. Their tissue study tests a low-cost idea that, if it works in people, could widen HIV prevention options greatly.
plos-pone-0002408:
Research by Roberge and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Christian Roberge, Simon Blanchet, Julian J. Dodson, and others. Its subject is disturbance of Social Hierarchy by an Invasive Species: A Gene Transcription Study. Ecological and evolutionary changes in native populations facing invasion by exotic species are increasingly reported.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002508:
Abraham and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from John M. Abraham, Yulan Cheng, James P. Hamilton, and others. Its subject is generation of Small 32 P-Labeled Peptides as a Potential Approach to Colorectal Cancer Therapy. Cancers have been revealed to be extremely heterogenous in terms of the frequency and types of mutations present in cells from different malignant tumors.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002608:
Led by Togbe, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Dieudonnée Togbe, Paulo Loureiro de Sousa, Mathilde Fauconnier, and others. Its subject is both Functional LTβ Receptor and TNF Receptor 2 Are Required for the Development of Experimental Cerebral Malaria. TNF-related lymphotoxin α (LTα) is key for the development of Plasmodium berghei ANKA (PbA)-induced experimental cerebral malaria (ECM).

The pathway involved has been attributed to TNFR2. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002708:
Work by Asaf Madi and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with genome holography: deciphering Function-Form motifs from gene expression data. Authorship is credited in the record to Asaf Madi and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. DNA chips allow simultaneous measurements of genome-wide response of thousands of genes, i.e. The authors add a further point. System level monitoring of the gene-network activity. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002808:
Research from Thomas G. Kaye and co-authors, published in PLOS ONE in 2008, covers dinosaurian soft tissues interpreted as bacterial biofilms. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Thomas G. Kaye, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. A scanning electron microscope survey was initiated to determine if the previously reported findings of “dinosaurian soft tissues” could be identified in situ within. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002908:
Fadi Bittar, Hervé Richet, Jean-Christophe Dubus and co-authors used molecular tests in 2008 to find germs in sputum from cystic fibrosis patients. Standard culture in the lab detects only a small share of the bacteria in these patients' airways. That leaves emerging pathogens easy to miss.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team applied DNA-based detection to sputum samples and found multiple emerging pathogens. Better detection matters because treatment in cystic fibrosis hinges on knowing which germs are present. The paper supports wider use of molecular methods alongside culture in routine care for these patients.
plos-pone-0003008:
Elizabeth Thompson and Andrew Travers studied a fly version of the Smyd4 protein in 2008. Smyd proteins, named for their SET and MYND domains, regulate transcription tied to cell growth and development in vertebrates. Their in vivo functions and mechanisms were poorly understood when the study began.

In Drosophila, the homologue acts as a muscle-specific transcriptional modulator involved in development, per the title. Using biochemical and genetic approaches together, the authors pinned down that role. Published in PLOS ONE, a defined fly model lets others dissect how this protein family steers muscle genes. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003108:
Debra Toiber, Amit Berson, David Greenberg and co-authors linked a variant of acetylcholinesterase to Alzheimer's features in 2008. Alzheimer's disease involves loss of cholinergic neurons and hyper-phosphorylation of the Tau protein. Both are hallmarks that any causal account should connect rather than treat separately.

Overexpression of an N-terminally extended synaptic variant, N-AChE-S, was causally involved in both phenomena in their tests, the authors report. Published in PLOS ONE, a single variant tying neuron loss to Tau change suggests a shared upstream step worth probing for therapy. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003208:
Paule Bénit, Sergio Goncalves, Emmanuel Philippe Dassa and colleagues study the Harlequin mouse as a disease model in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Despite progress in knowledge of the molecular bases of mitochondrial diseases, no effective treatments had been made. Faithful animal models would be very helpful for designing such treatments. The team had shown earlier that the Harlequin mouse carries just such a defect.

They report that variability of the Harlequin phenotype resembles that of human mitochondrial complex I deficiency syndromes. Readers learn why the model's uneven symptoms are a strength, since human disease also varies widely. A model that matches human variability can test treatments more honestly.
plos-pone-0003308:
Jana Sponarova, Sofia N. Nyström and Gunilla T. Westermark test transfer of amyloidosis by blood cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Spongiform encephalopathies have been reported to be transmitted by blood transfusion even prior to clinical onset. Experimental AA-amyloidosis shows similarities with prion disease, and amyloid-containing organ extracts can prime a recipient for the disease.

The title reports that AA-amyloidosis can be transferred by peripheral blood monocytes. Readers learn that mobile blood cells can carry amyloid seeding ability. That finding matters for transfusion safety and for how systemic amyloid disease spreads in the body.
plos-pone-0007408: Fatty liver can progress toward cirrhosis and liver cancer, and this study mapped exactly where different chemicals sit inside diseased liver tissue. Using two high-powered microscopes — one using synchrotron infrared light, one firing ions at the sample — the team drew chemical images of the fat deposits. Seeing the molecular layout in place reveals details about how the disease develops that bulk tests miss.
plos-pone-0007508: Fighting a parasite costs energy that could go to growth, and this study used a mathematical model to untangle the trade-off. It combined an animal's genetic potential for growth, its disease resistance, and its nutrition to predict how infections with tiny parasites play out. The model helps explain why well-fed animals still sometimes lose the battle.
plos-pone-0007608: Ewing sarcoma, a childhood bone cancer, is driven by a rogue fusion protein called EWS/FLI1. This study shows it acts largely through GLI1, a signaling protein better known from other cancers. Identifying GLI1 as the middleman exposes a new target for treating this aggressive tumor of the young.
plos-pone-0007708: Stem cells were pictured as either pluripotent or committed, with nothing in between. This study of human embryonic stem cells found instead a continuum of states bridging the two. The gradient view replaces the on-off switch with a sliding scale of potential.
plos-pone-0007808: Campbell's monkeys tweak their alarm calls with prefixes and suffixes — the animal equivalent of affixation. This study documented the monkeys changing call meaning by adding sound units. The finding pushes the roots of language-like structure deep into primate evolution.
plos-pone-0007908: Lab-grown skin got a cancer-gene invasion. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Vaughan's team showed H-Ras turns skin cells invasive in lab skin. Ras also cranks collagen-chewing enzymes. The invasion model was built. The test feeds cancer biology.
plos-pone-0008008: The stress sensor PERK drives both normal insulin cells and their tumors. This mouse study showed PERK regulates the growth of insulin-secreting beta-cell tumors in the pancreas. The kinase is a double-edged sword — essential for health, exploited by cancer.
plos-pone-0008108: Gonorrhea needs a vaccine, and its shape-shifting Opa proteins are targets. This study characterized antibodies against the proteins' loops — including a conserved one that could anchor a vaccine. The functional map guides antigen selection.
plos-pone-0008208: Chronic viruses outrun the immune system, but engineered T cells could catch up. This study built antigen-specific T cells from modified human blood stem cells in immunodeficient mice. The humanized model advances cell therapy for persistent infections.
plos-pone-0008308: Colon cancers with stable genomes still break the activin growth-brake. This study showed genetic plus epigenetic hits disrupt activin signaling in microsatellite-stable tumors. The double assault reveals an alternative route to the same malignant end.
plos-pone-0008408: Frog plague outcomes were tied to temperature. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Ribas's team profiled amphibian gene responses to the chytrid fungus across temperatures. Not all species face equal risk. The temperature-tuned profiles explain the patchy toll. The data guide conservation triage.
plos-pone-0008508: A tularemia germ got a tiny-RNA tell. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Cremer's team caught miR-155 rising in mild but not vicious Francisella. The tell-tale split was mapped. The tell feeds immune science.
plos-pone-0008608: State bird lists got a conservation audit. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Wells's team compared global versus local focus of U.S. state endangered-bird lists. Local priorities can miss global needs. The paradox was quantified. The audit steers smarter conservation.
plos-pone-0008708: Desert mice's camouflage got a pigment recipe. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Singaravelan's team showed spiny mice tune eumelanin-to-pheomelanin ratios for cryptic coloration in Evolution Canyon. The canyon's two slopes demand different coats. The pigment dial was mapped. The recipe reveals selection at work.
plos-pone-0008808: Immune presenters got an alarm boost. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Frei's team showed MHC class II molecules enhance Toll-like receptor innate responses. The presenter-alarm crosstalk was mapped. The boost reveals immune teamwork.
plos-pone-0008908: Chromosome caps' repair enzymes got a G4 test. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Vallur and Maizels compared EXO1 and FEN1 activities at telomeric G4 DNA. The distinct cut patterns were mapped. The test informs telomere biology.
plos-pone-0009008: DNA repair's tag got a live view. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Batters's team visualized PCNA monoubiquitination in vivo with single-pass spectral FRET. The damage-bypass signal was filmed. The view informs DNA-repair science.
plos-pone-0009108: Tiny graspers got a shape-memory test. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Lejeune's team tested preemie grasping and shape memory. The tiny hands' recall was logged. The test feeds baby science. The recall held across the preemie group.
plos-pone-0009208: Sunlight sneezes got a brain-wave read. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Langer's team used EEG to find neural bases of photic sneezing. The light-sneeze circuits were mapped. The read explains a quirky reflex.
plos-pone-0009308: Monkey brains were shown to blend senses and rewards when deciding. This 2010 PLOS ONE study by Rorie and colleagues recorded lateral intraparietal cortex neurons in macaques integrating sensory and reward information during perceptual decisions. While LIP was known to carry both signal types, how they combine was unknown. The integration reveals how value biases what the eyes report.
plos-pone-0011408: Ovarian cancer scrambles the genome, deleting or duplicating chunks of DNA in patterns that drive the disease. This research paper scans those copy-number changes and finds new interactions between distant genomic regions. Linking far-apart loci into cooperating pairs gives researchers fresh suspects in how the cancer's genetic chaos translates into aggressive tumors.
plos-pone-0011508: The brain adapts to mental conflict — but must it notice the conflict first? This research paper shows that conflict adaptation can be triggered unconsciously, without awareness. The finding pushes a supposedly high-level control process down into the automatic machinery, blurring the line between deliberate and reflexive mind.
plos-pone-0011608: Aphids are tiny, numerous, and evolutionarily restless. This research paper combines body measurements, family trees, and trait evolution in the species-rich genus Aphis. The three-way analysis shows how form and lineage dance together across hundreds of aphid species.
plos-pone-0011708: T cells pass 'go' signals along webs of touching proteins. This research paper names ADAP as the central hub where phosphate-tagged proteins meet in T cells. The hub reveals the switchboard wiring behind immune activation — a control room for defense.
plos-pone-0011808: Mussels clustered on sunken whale bones host helpful bacteria — some inside their cells, some outside. This research paper studies both lifestyles in one mussel species and traces evolution's drift from outer to inner living. The shift shows partnerships moving house, into the cell.
plos-pone-0011908: Epstein-Barr virus sabotages the immune alarm. This research paper shows EBV blocks the buildup of interferon-alpha secretion by switching on SOCS3 in human monocytes. The sabotage reveals exactly how the virus muffles the body's early warning system in people.
plos-pone-0012108: High salt triggers a cellular defense — and MDC1 helps flip the switch. This research paper shows mediator of DNA damage checkpoint 1 contributes to salt-induced activation of the osmoprotective factor TonEBP/OREBP. The salt-defense link reveals cross-talk between DNA repair and osmosis.
plos-pone-0012208: Membrane fusion happens in the right place at the right time. This research paper shows spatial regulation of membrane fusion is controlled by modification of lipid signals. The lipid-signaling control reveals fusion's address system, today and always, for good measure, worldwide.
plos-pone-0012308: Losing stemness tracks rising nuclear zinc. This research paper shows loss of pluripotency in human embryonic stem cells directly correlates with an increase in nuclear zinc. The zinc-pluripotency link reveals a stemness marker, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012408: Malaria drugs slow the parasite's blood cycle and wake drug pumps. This research paper shows anti-malaria exposure delays the Plasmodium falciparum red-blood-cell cycle and drives drug transporter gene expression. The delay finding reveals malaria drug resistance, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012508: Coral and its algae trade superoxide outside their cells. This research paper studies extracellular production and degradation of superoxide in a coral and cultured Symbiodinium. The superoxide cycling reveals coral-oxidant biology, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012608: Depth vision survives without the lateral occipital cortex. This research paper studies stereoscopic vision in the absence of the lateral occipital cortex. The vision finding reveals a brain-plasticity proof, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012708: New twists in insect mitochondrial genome asymmetry. This research paper presents new views on strand asymmetry in insect mitochondrial genomes. The asymmetry findings reveal a genome-evolution clue, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012808: Zebrafish sperm-stem-cell niches and transplants. This research paper studies sperm stem cell niche and sperm stem cell transplantation in zebrafish. The niche finding reveals a fish-fertility system, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.

thompson-semitic-magic-1908:
R. Campbell Thompson, a British Museum curator, published Semitic Magic in 1908. He surveyed magical practice across the ancient Near East and traced its growth. Assyrian, Hebrew, and Arabic traditions all pass through his account.

Thompson draws on cuneiform tablets that few Western readers knew existed. Exorcisms, charms, and folk rites show traditions borrowing from one another. He asks where practices began and how they traveled between peoples. The survey pioneered a map of Semitic magical traditions as one connected field. Later scholarship corrected details but kept his broad frame. Thompson's museum work with tablets gave the book unusual firsthand authority.
topsell-historie-serpents-1608:
Edward Topsell followed his book of beasts with The Historie of Serpents in 1608. The two volumes belong together as his great survey of the animal world. This one covers snakes and everything his age counted as a serpent, real or rumored.

Dragons and basilisks share the pages with vipers and common adders. Topsell gives each creature's look, its poison, its cures, and the morals it teaches. Drawings show winged serpents as calmly as garden snakes. The book is a cabinet of scaled wonders from Renaissance England. Readers learn as much about the fears of 1608 as about snakes.
guazzo-compendium-maleficarum-latin-1608:
Francesco Maria Guazzo, a Milanese priest, published the Compendium Maleficarum in Latin at Milan in 1608. Three books gather the lore and practice of witchcraft into one compendium, a summary of the whole dark subject. This text is the Latin original from which the library's 1929 English translation was made.

Guazzo describes the pact with the devil, the sabbath, and the marks left on witches' bodies. He draws on trial records and on the demonologists before him. Woodcuts in the original printing show the sabbath in grim detail. The compendium served priests and judges as a reference work. Having the Latin source lets readers check the famous translation against its original voice.
perkins-discourse-damned-art-english-160:
William Perkins, the great Puritan theologian of Cambridge, wrote his Discourse of the Damned Art of Witchcraft late in life, and it appeared in 1608. Perkins sets out witchcraft so far as Scripture reveals it, no further and no less. His becomes the most influential English Reformed demonology of the age.

He defines the witch by her covenant with the devil. Good and bad witches alike fall under his condemnation, a hard point against village healers. His verdicts are measured in tone and severe in effect. Generations of English ministers preached Perkins on this subject. The book shows Puritan theology giving the witch trial its most respectable English foundation.
